name: Aaron Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. What is a normal workday on your crew?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43, with a two-year technical diploma, and I lead the electricity company's ridge repair crew. We load climbing gear before dawn and head to poles a bucket truck cannot reach; I like teaching the apprentices how to read rotten timber. The drive on icy roads and the low pay for a lead job wear me down.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And what is home like, and how do you use new tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Priya takes childcare bookings at home, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. Her income varies; we have less than one month of expenses saved and only a few other line employers within reach. I am good at this work, but I have never used an AI tool and I prefer the test meter and my own eyes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the paperwork may get faster, but our lines still cross steep ground that machines cannot wish flat. The ridge power line still needs an apprentice who knows the pole before the screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the work, I'd be relieved. For home, less than one month's savings and my wife Priya's changing childcare bookings keep me worried, even if no new machine arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep leading the ridge repair crew and check the rope, ground and isolation myself each morning. From the next wage, we'll send the price of one weekly takeaway to the mortgage-payment buffer until it covers a full payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about bills, not about a sudden AI takeover. The children's school costs arrive whether our van needs repairs or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which pole would you use to train an apprentice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start with the old timber pole on High Path, where the truck cannot turn round. The apprentice must inspect the grain and set the climbing gear before I let anyone lift a conductor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the weekly saving leave untouched?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One takeaway a week is small, but it is money from a wage we actually receive. Priya and I would keep the children's school meals and put the new saving aside on pay day.

say: **Ridge repairs** still require a trained crew even when office paperwork gets quicker.
An **apprentice** should learn the pole and isolation steps before relying on a screen.
think: I expect my **lead lineworker job** to continue in this picture.
Our **thin savings** and uncertain childcare bookings make ordinary bills stressful anyway.
do: **Keep** leading ridge repairs and check rope, ground and isolation every morning.
**Save** one weekly takeaway cost from new wages toward a mortgage-payment buffer.
feel: **Anxious** about home expenses despite confidence in the work.
S0.quote: The ridge power line still needs an apprentice who knows the pole before the screen.
fieldNote: He speaks with **craft pride**, but his private worry is the household balance each month.
He describes **new saving from wages**, small enough to protect school meals.

steps.text: Keep leading ridge repairs and checking rope and isolation
Save weekly takeaway cost from new wages for mortgage buffer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI can book crews and write orders, but dispatch should call us before sending a truck up a closed ridge road. I do not want a machine deciding that a risky climb fits into an extra half hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hands-on work may last, yet faster schedules could cut our standby hours. Those hours make up for low base pay in this depot, and there are few other line crews within a reasonable drive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask dispatch to read back the route and isolation order before every winter call. At the first company meeting on AI scheduling, I'll bring three cases where the road was blocked and ask the supervisor to keep a human check before assigning a climb.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and irritated at the thought of explaining the hills to an office program. If standby pay falls, the mortgage does not fall with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do at the closed ridge road?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would call control and stop the crew at the junction, then get a new route from someone who knows the closure. I would not ask the truck driver to try an iced lane because the screen says open. A computer's open road cannot carry our power-line truck through an iced ridge lane.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you prove standby pay has fallen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare the next three pay slips with the same season last year and mark the standby hours. If they drop, Priya and I would cut the sports subscription first, not the children's lunches.

say: **Dispatch AI** should still leave a human check on winter routes and isolation orders.
A climb cannot be safely squeezed into a **shorter schedule** just because software says so.
think: My **physical linework** may survive, but standby pay could shrink under tighter scheduling.
Few **nearby line jobs** leave little room if this depot reduces hours.
do: **Read back** routes and isolation orders with dispatch before winter callouts.
**Bring** three blocked-road examples to the supervisor's scheduling meeting.
feel: **Anxious** about standby pay and the pressure to rush hills work.
S1.quote: A computer's open road cannot carry our power-line truck through an iced ridge lane.
fieldNote: He resists the software but offers **specific blocked-road evidence** rather than only objecting.
Standby hours matter because **base pay is low** and local alternatives are scarce.

steps.text: Read back winter routes and isolation orders before callouts
Bring three blocked-road examples to company scheduling meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the depot thinking AI by 2028 might replace much of dispatch and ordering, but robots that can climb and repair arrive around 2031. I would ask exactly which paid crews will remain for storm nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have taught apprentices for years and know these ridges, but the employer can still choose fewer people. We have under one month saved and Priya's home childcare depends on parents' bookings; I could not wait calmly for a redundancy letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomorrow I'll ask the depot manager for the 2028 dispatch plan and the 2031 field staffing plan. Priya and I will drop the paid television package and send that amount from each new wage to the emergency account; if a formal cut is announced, I'll apply to the few line crews farther down the valley.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, especially about the mortgage. I can repair a power line after a storm, but I cannot repair a missing pay packet before the mortgage date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the children hear at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the children we are cutting the television package and keeping school and food as usual. I would not frighten them with a claim that my crew is already gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for training or leave immediately?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask a neighbouring contractor about a real vacancy before leaving my depot. I would not spend our last savings on robot tuition unless an employer paid for it and offered a line of work afterward.

say: **2028 thinking AI** may change dispatch before capable field robots reach line repairs around 2031.
The company should name **paid storm crews** rather than promise vague future work.
think: My **lead skills** may not protect a crew if the employer chooses fewer workers.
Under **one month saved**, we cannot wait long if a line wage disappears.
do: **Ask** management for separate 2028 dispatch and 2031 field staffing plans.
**Cancel** the television package and cut that recurring spending.
**Save** its monthly cost from new wages in an emergency account.
feel: **Alarmed** about losing the line wage before the next mortgage payment.
S2.quote: I can repair a power line after a storm, but I cannot repair a missing pay packet before the mortgage date.
fieldNote: His slow adoption of AI meets a **very short financial runway** in the fast scenario.
He would seek a **real vacancy** only after a formal cut; leaving now would expose the mortgage.
The television cancellation funds **new saving** from subsequent wages.

steps.text: Ask manager for 2028 dispatch and 2031 field staffing plans
Cancel paid television package and cut its recurring charge
Save television cost from each new wage in emergency account
Apply to valley line crews if a formal cut is announced

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years allows the company to test field robots on a ridge line before putting people out of work around 2034. The thinking AI in 2031 changes the control desk earlier; the crew should still be called when a storm drops wire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could be useful teaching safe climbs or checking robot rigging, but I am not going to assume there is a paid post. The mortgage is due every month while the company talks about what might exist in eight years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask for a paid observation day when the company runs a ridge robot trial, if one is offered. I will record where the machine fails on rock or ice, then take those notes to a staff meeting before any change in crew rosters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though five years gives me room to argue from what I have seen. I still dislike learning a machine simply to prove my own work mattered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What site would make the robot test honest?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make the trial use the narrow High Path turn and an old pole, with a crew ready to stop the job. A sunny robot trial in the depot yard cannot show who repairs a ridge power line in ice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you attend a trial on your own time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would attend on paid time because that is still work for the electricity company. If there is no paid observation place, I will keep my regular repairs and ask for the written trial results.

say: **Ridge trials** need rock, ice and old poles before field robots arrive around 2034.
**Human crews** should keep storm work after thinking AI changes control desks in 2031.
think: A paid **rigging or teaching role** might fit me, but the company has offered none.
Our **mortgage** cannot wait through years of unpaid preparation.
do: **Attend** a paid ridge robot observation day if the company offers one.
**Record** field failures on rock and ice for the next staffing meeting.
feel: **Anxious** about eventual hours, despite more time to collect evidence.
S3.quote: A sunny robot trial in the depot yard cannot show who repairs a ridge power line in ice.
fieldNote: He will observe a robot on **paid time**, while remaining reluctant to operate one.
His test criteria come from **winter terrain** and an old pole rather than a general fear of machines.

steps.text: Attend paid ridge robot observation day if company offers one
Record robot failures on rock and ice for staffing meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to teach a full generation of apprentices before capable robots reach field work around 2039. Thinking AI in 2036 may change the planning desk first, and the employer should say how it will keep experienced crews paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 56 by the robot date and might still climb if my knees allow it. I would consider a paid training job for apprentices, but the company has not offered one and our thin savings make retirement guesses foolish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep my technical diploma and line safety tickets current, and ask once a year whether the electricity company has a paid apprentice trainer vacancy. Priya and I will keep sending the saved television cost from each pay packet to the emergency account, stopping only if childcare bookings fall enough that the bills need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about this month's money, even with a decade to prepare for robots. I can be hopeful about passing on the craft and worried about the next mortgage payment at once. A decade before line-repair robots arrive will not make our next mortgage payment for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your son about this trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show my son how an apprentice checks a pole and tell him to choose his own work when the time comes. I would not promise him that a training place will exist in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a trainer post a real alternative?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The job would need a full wage, paid hours and proper field teaching, not one day showing schoolchildren a harness. If such a vacancy opens, I would apply before giving up regular line shifts.

say: **Ten years** allow apprentices to learn field safety before capable robots arrive around 2039.
The electricity company should publish **paid crew plans** before 2036 thinking AI changes planning desks.
think: A paid **apprentice trainer post** might fit at 56, but no offer exists.
Our **thin savings** make current bills urgent regardless of a distant robot date.
do: **Renew** technical and line safety tickets while keeping regular repair shifts.
**Ask** annually about full-wage apprentice trainer vacancies with field teaching.
**Save** cancelled television costs from new pay while childcare bookings cover bills.
feel: **Anxious** about current household bills, with hope for a later teaching role.
S4.quote: A decade before line-repair robots arrive will not make our next mortgage payment for us.
fieldNote: He sees **teaching apprentices** as a possible later role, conditional on a full paid vacancy.
Even the longest runway leaves him **anxious now** because of low pay and little savings.
His ongoing saving pauses if **childcare income** falls below household bills.

steps.text: Renew line safety tickets and keep regular ridge repair shifts
Ask annually about full-wage apprentice trainer vacancy
Save television cost from new pay while childcare bookings cover bills

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because dispatch changes quickly and capable field robots come around 2031, when we have barely any money to bridge a lost wage. A clear crew plan and a full paid trainer post, if the company offers one, would let me decide without guessing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens to the apprentice when a robot takes the first easy climb. My crew can still teach a safe test, but it needs paid hours on real poles. I cannot feed my family with a promise that somebody may need a power-line trainer later.

headlineQuote: I cannot feed my family with a promise that somebody may need a power-line trainer later.
portrait: **Aaron**, 43, leads difficult ridge line repairs and teaches apprentices after a two-year technical diploma.
His **low pay**, variable childcare income, mortgage and under-one-month reserve keep bills tight despite high skill.
He has **never used AI** and trusts physical tests, yet would observe a paid robot trial on real winter terrain.
A future **trainer post** interests him only with full wages and actual field teaching hours.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves little time or savings before capable line robots arrive around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: A clear **crew plan** and a full paid trainer vacancy, if available, would give him a real choice.
